answer.label: Not Walt Disney — actually Walter J. Hickel
answer.authorDates: 1919–2010 · Two-term governor of Alaska & U.S. Secretary of the Interior
answer.sourceLine: The line belongs to Alaska governor Walter J. “Wally” Hickel, who said it while defending his state’s aerial wolf-control program — the Anchorage Daily News traces it to a 1992 NBC interview, and it was collected in the 1994 book The Wit and Wisdom of Wally Hickel. Wikiquote lists it under Misattributed on its Walt Disney page; Disney died in 1966, decades before the remark is documented.
answer.confidenceText: Firmly credited to Hickel by Wikiquote and by his hometown paper’s obituary — though sources disagree on whether the line was first spoken in 1992 or first printed in 1994.

source.excerpt: You can’t just let nature run wild.
trail: The anchor. Wikiquote files this line under Misattributed on its Walt Disney page ↗, with the entry: “Walter Joseph Hickel, on the killing of wolves, as quoted in Living With Wolves (2005) by James Dutcher. p. 8.” Quote Investigator has no article on this quote, so Wikiquote’s sourced entry is the best existing research.

1992 — the remark. The Anchorage Daily News obituary ↗ reports that Hickel made the assertion “you can’t just let nature run wild” in a 1992 NBC interview about the state’s aerial predator-control program, and that environmentalists criticized him for it. His hometown paper’s editorial send-off ↗ noted the line “became an instant classic.”

1994 — into print, with a wrinkle. A competing account: the obituary carried by the History News Network ↗ says “‘You can’t just let nature run wild,’ he wrote in a 1994 book, ‘The Wit and Wisdom of Wally Hickel.’” The Alaska State Library catalogs that book ↗ as compiled and edited by Malcolm B. Roberts (Anchorage: Searchers Press, 1994, 239p.), describing it only as the former governor’s “short takes.” That those short takes were spoken comes from the Anchorage Daily News, which describes the book ↗ as more than 200 pages of remarks Roberts jotted down as the two travelled together — which likely reconciles the two accounts.

2015 — the correction. Matt Novak included the line in “8 Walt Disney Quotes That Are Actually Fake” ↗, calling it “a joke from Walter J. Hickel” and admitting he could not explain how Disney’s name got attached — speculating only that Disney’s theme parks “epitomize absolute control over one’s environment.”
source.excerptNote: No transcript of the 1992 NBC broadcast appears to be online, so the line survives through news reporting, obituaries, and quote collections rather than a retrievable primary recording. Every documented version is this one short sentence — there is no known fuller passage around it.

source.rightsNote: This is a modern remark, not an old text. The wording is documented from a 1992 broadcast interview and collected in a 1994 book — both far later than the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff, so nothing here is public domain. Quoting a single short sentence with attribution is ordinary fair use, but the collection it appears in remains under copyright.

author.name: Walter J. Hickel
author.heading: The man who actually said it
author.metaLine: 1919–2010 · Governor of Alaska (1966–1969, 1990–1994) & U.S. Secretary of the Interior
author.bio: Walter J. “Wally” Hickel was an Alaska construction magnate turned politician who served two non-consecutive terms as governor and, in between, spent some 22 months as Richard Nixon’s Secretary of the Interior before being fired in November 1970 for publicly breaking with the president over Vietnam. He was known for blunt, off-the-cuff aphorisms that his longtime aide Malcolm B. Roberts collected ↗ on “the backs of envelopes, airplane napkins and whatever else I could lay my hands on.” “You can’t just let nature run wild” is the most famous of them — a line his critics treated as self-refuting and his defenders read as pragmatism about active wildlife management.

cite.sourceCitation: Walter J. Hickel, quoted in "Former Alaska Gov. Hickel dead at 90," Anchorage Daily News, May 8, 2010 — remark made in a 1992 NBC interview on Alaska's aerial predator-control program. Collected in Malcolm B. Roberts, comp. and ed., The Wit and Wisdom of Wally Hickel (Anchorage: Searchers Press, 1994). Listed as misattributed to Walt Disney in Wikiquote, "Walt Disney," Misattributed section, citing Living With Wolves (2005) by James Dutcher, p. 8.

misattribution.heading: How Walt Disney got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook case of a line drifting to a more famous name. Hickel was a regional politician remembered mainly in Alaska; Disney is one of the internet’s biggest quote magnets. The quote industry made the swap and then cited itself.

items.why: AZQuotes ↗ and Quotefancy ↗ both credit the line to Disney and both supply no source whatsoever — no film, book, speech, or date. That sourceless pattern is the tell. Wikiquote, by contrast, puts it in the Misattributed section ↗ of its Disney page.

Disney died in December 1966. The remark is documented from a 1992 NBC interview ↗ about an Alaska wolf-control program that did not exist in Disney’s lifetime. This is a plain observation from the two confirmed dates, not a claim made by either source.

items.scope: Even the corrections get it half-wrong
items.why: Fact-checks that rescue the quote from Disney often identify Hickel only as “the Interior Secretary for President Richard Nixon” ↗. True of the man, but not of the moment: he held that post in 1969–70, and said this line roughly two decades later as governor of Alaska ↗ during his 1990–94 term.

misattribution.truthLine: It was a governor defending a wolf cull, not a filmmaker musing about imagination — and Wikiquote has said so plainly ↗ for years while the quote sites kept printing Disney’s name.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Hickel returned to the Alaska governorship in 1990, and by 1992 his administration was pushing an aerial predator-control program — shooting wolves from aircraft to boost moose and caribou numbers for hunters. The backlash was national. Pressed to defend the policy on NBC, Hickel produced the sentence that outlived everything else in his long public career.

The line was meant as common sense: wildlife populations, in his view, required active management rather than benign neglect. It landed as something closer to a punchline. The Anchorage Daily News ↗ noted in its editorial farewell that the line “became an instant classic” — not the kind of classic that ends up on bronze plaques.
context.detailsSummary: The phrase’s afterlife in Alaska politics
detailsBody: Three decades on, the sentence is still the shorthand for Alaska’s predator policy — usually deployed by the people Hickel was arguing against. Conservation lawyers have made it a headline: a 2017 piece by Peter Van Tuyn, published by the American College of Environmental Lawyers ↗ and republished by Trustees for Alaska ↗, takes it as its title to frame a critique of the state’s ongoing practice of culling bears and wolves to maximize game species.
There is a quiet irony in the Disney mix-up. Hickel’s line was an argument for engineering the wilderness — and the name it got pinned on belongs to the man who built Frontierland.
context.pull: It was meant as common sense. It landed as a punchline — and outlived everything else he ever said.
